title: Evaluating and Discussing Trade-offs
summary: Defending a design under pushback: naming what every LLD decision costs and buys, absorbing curveball features without a rewrite, and engaging with disagreement instead of digging in.

slides.markdown:
The final stretch of an LLD interview isn't about having the "right" design — there usually isn't one — it's about defending the design you built under real pushback. Every decision you made, a Strategy interface, a checked exception, a has-a relationship, traded something for something else, and naming that trade-off is what separates a design that was reasoned about from one that just happened.

This topic covers narrating trade-offs, absorbing curveball features without a rewrite, and engaging with pushback instead of defending a design rigidly.

slides.sectionTitle: Why every LLD decision is a trade-off, and saying the trade-off out loud
slides.markdown:
Every design choice buys something at a cost: a pricing-strategy interface buys extensibility at the cost of an extra layer of indirection for a reader tracing the code; a checked exception buys explicit caller handling at the cost of more verbose call sites. There is no trade-off-free choice — only choices whose cost you've acknowledged versus ones you haven't.

Saying it out loud matters as much as making the right call: "I chose composition here, which costs a bit more boilerplate than inheritance but means I can swap pricing rules without touching Vehicle" tells the interviewer you weighed the option, even if they'd have leaned differently.

Interviewers rarely fail a candidate for the specific choice — they fail candidates who can't explain why they made it.

slides.sectionTitle: Handling "now add feature X" curveballs without a full redesign
slides.markdown:
When the interviewer says "now add subscription-based parking with a monthly cap," the instinct to panic and redesign from scratch is the wrong response. First, check whether an existing seam absorbs it: if pricing is already behind a strategy interface, a new subscription strategy is a new class, not a rewrite.

If no seam exists, say so honestly and make the smallest change that accommodates the feature — extending one class or adding one new collaborator — rather than restructuring everything defensively. A design that needs a moderate, explainable change under a curveball is normal and expected; the interviewer is testing whether you can extend calmly, not whether your first draft was flawless.

Narrate your check: "does my current pricing interface cover this, or do I need a new concept?" — that question is itself a demonstration of the skill.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: extending a working design for a new requirement without breaking existing classes
Discussing complexity/testability/performance trade-offs of a chosen pattern
slides.markdown:
When defending a pattern choice, be ready to name its cost in three dimensions: **complexity** — a strategy interface adds a layer a reader must trace through; **testability** — usually improves, since each strategy is testable in isolation without instantiating the whole `ParkingLot`; and **performance** — an extra virtual call per invocation, almost always negligible compared to the flexibility gained.

A strong answer names the dimension where the cost is real and the one where it's not: "the complexity cost is real — a new engineer has to learn the strategy indirection — but the performance cost is not, this isn't a hot loop." A weak answer either claims no cost exists, or lists costs without weighing which ones matter here.

This is the skill interviewers are checking for in the trade-offs step: can you reason about cost with precision, not just gesture at "trade-offs exist."

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: two valid designs for the same prompt, and how to argue for one
slides.markdown:
| | Design A: strategy interface for pricing | Design B: single calculator with a switch statement |
|---|---|---|
| Extensibility | New vehicle type = new class, no edits | New vehicle type = new case, edits existing code |
| Simplicity for 2-3 fixed cases | Slightly more ceremony | Simpler to read for a small, fixed set |
| Testability | Each strategy tested in isolation | One class tests all cases together |
| Best when | Pricing rules are expected to grow or vary often | Pricing rules are small, fixed, and unlikely to change |

**How to argue for one:** anchor the argument in the stated or implied growth of the requirement, not a general preference for "clean code." If the prompt hinted at more vehicle types coming, argue for A and name B's edit cost as the reason; if the domain is genuinely fixed, arguing for B and calling out A as premature abstraction is equally valid.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: defending a design rigidly instead of engaging with the interviewer's pushback
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I designed this carefully, so I should defend every part of it exactly as originally proposed."

**Why it's wrong:** treating pushback as an attack to repel, rather than new information to weigh, reads as inflexibility — a trait interviewers actively screen against, since real design work involves constant renegotiation with teammates and requirements. Rigid defense also wastes time relitigating a minor point instead of moving the interview forward.

**Correct model:** engage with pushback as a genuine question — "that's a fair point, here's why I still lean this way" or "actually, you're right, I'd adjust it to..." Conceding a specific point when the interviewer has a better argument is a stronger signal than defending everything reflexively; it shows judgment, not just conviction.
